title: AI in Praxis
text:
Where AI Helps…  and Where It Doesn’t (Yet)

University standards require:

Integrity — no plagiarism or data fabrication.
Originality — ideas must be your own.
Transparency — disclose AI use if required by policy.

AI can assist with:

Rapid literature discovery

Structuring outlines, abstracts, and drafts

Grammar, tone, and citation checks.

Generating sample code or figures from your notes.

AI cannot replace:

Reading and understanding papers.

Critical judgment or design reasoning.

Ethical authorship or data verification.








Tip


Use AI to speed tasks — not to skip thinking.







Where AI Helps — and Where It Doesn’t.
Explain that AI tools act like accelerators, not replacements for academic skills.
Give one concrete example: “If you ask for key papers, always verify titles and DOIs before citing.”
Mention that AI may misread visuals or produce generic text if prompts are vague.
Emphasise that the human remains the researcher; AI does the mechanical side.
Conclude: “We’ll explore how to balance speed and scholarship in today’s session.”
Segment timing: 5–15 min
Learning Outcomes linked: LO #1 (Search & curate), LO #2 (Synthesize literature), LO #3 (Draft with AI) — Knowledge phase
Facilitator task: deliver a 10-minute talk with examples, show a one-page cheat-sheet or diagram of the research lifecycle.

Creating Prompts
Build and refine LLM prompts for literature discovery.

What is a prompt?
A short instruction or question you give to an AI model.
It guides the model’s task, scope, and format of response.

Find 10 peer-reviewed papers from 2018–2025  
on sustainable or green product design, development, or engineering.  
Include title, author, year, DOI, and one-line summary.  
Mark any uncertain citation with [VERIFY].

Prompt structure

Role – tell the AI who it should act as.

Task – describe exactly what to do.

Context / criteria – add limits or filters.

Output format – specify how results should appear.

Optimise Your Prompt with the LLM
You can also ask the LLM to co-create or optimise the prompt with you.

You are an academic search assistant helping me locate recent, peer-reviewed papers.
Improve my prompt for clarity and reproducibility.

Keep all key terms and add filters for:
    •   peer-reviewed journals
    •   date range (2018–present)
    •   output format (table)
Return your optimised version.

Build and refine LLM prompts for literature discovery.

Detailed Prompt Sample

You are a research assistant helping me locate recent, peer-reviewed papers.
Topic focus: [YOUR TOPIC]

Please do the following:
1. Return a list of **10 peer-reviewed journal articles from 2018 onwards**.  
2. For each article, include:
   - Title  
   - Author(s)  
   - Year  
   - DOI or publisher link  
   - A **one-sentence summary** of the study’s aim or contribution.  
3. Exclude:
   - Preprints, blogs, or non-peer-reviewed sources  
   - Duplicates or incomplete references  
4. If uncertain about any citation, mark it with `[VERIFY]` instead of guessing a DOI.  
5. Present the output as a simple table.

Example output format:
| # | Title | Author(s) | Year | DOI | Summary |  
|---|--------|------------|------|------|----------|  
| 1 | ... | ... | ... | ... | ... |

Respond only with verifiable results.

The Deaf Leading the Blind: What Silicon Valley’s LLM’s Cannot See

“…They have mouths, but cannot speak, eyes, but cannot see. They have ears, but cannot hear, noses, but cannot smell… Those who make them will be like them, and so will all who trust in them.” (Psalm 115:4–8, NIV)

I recently found myself watching See No Evil, Hear No Evil on Youtube, drawn in by the “I am white” clip with Richard Pryor (Figure 1). It is a minor 1989 comedy. The hilarious Pryor plays Wally, a blind man who refuses to acknowledge that he is blind. Gene Wilder plays Dave, a deaf man who has become remarkably good at pretending to hear. Together they blunder through a murder mystery, each borrowing the faculty of the other. Wally strides into bar brawls while Dave shouts directions. Dave borrows Wally’s ears to detect approaching sirens. The comedy turns on the gap between performed and actual perception (Figure 2). On reflection, it could be a surprisingly accurate description of artificial intelligence (AI), specifically visual-focussed Large Language Models (LLM).







Figure 1: In this subway sequence, Wally (Pryor) performs “simulated sight”, using memorized cues to mask his blindness.








Figure 2: During the job interview, Wally and Dave attempt to communicate across a complete sensory disconnect.




The joke, as these things go, has aged rather well. Silicon Valley has spent the better part of a decade equipping AI with eyes. Visual encoders. Camera inputs. The image-upload button is presented to us with confidence that the machine can now see. What the product announcements rarely discuss is the architecture sitting behind the lens. The LLMs process visual information by first converting it into words; then reasoning about those words; and, finally describing what they believe to be there. All with the practiced confidence of a man who cannot see the bar fight he has just walked into.


The Wally Problem
Silicon Valley’s flagship general-purpose LLMs still have the language bottleneck firmly in place. The chatbot works, ostensibly, because the partnership is all it has. This appears to be a Wally problem. Vision for most multimodal AI systems relies on a process of narration, not perception. Pixels enter; the language model converts them into tokens; the tokens are then reasoned about (Su et al., 2025). Under light cognitive load, this works well enough. Under heavier demands requiring genuine inference, the visual attention collapses, and the model does what researchers have delicately termed “relying on linguistic priors” (Qian et al., 2026). It does a Wally. It narrates the world it expects rather than the one in front of it. In other words, it does not merely struggle to see. It hallucinates with pre-trained confidence.

Qian, Z., Ma, Y., Ouyang, Z., Wang, Z., Xu, Z., Luo, F., Liu, X., Ge, Z., Guo, Y., & Han, J. (2026). Cognitive pivot points and visual anchoring: Unveiling and rectifying hallucinations in multimodal reasoning models. arXiv Preprint arXiv:2604.10219. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10219


But what about Tesla?
An instinctive counter-argument could be to point to Tesla. If the LLM cannot see, how then is a two-tonne vehicle able to negotiate Californian roads without incident? The answer is not that Tesla has solved the vision problem. The Tesla v12 architecture maps pixels directly to steering and braking outputs, bypassing language altogether. There is no Dave whispering directions to Wally here. The blind man has simply been removed. The car does not name a stop sign before responding to it; it encodes the sign as a spatial object with associated coordinates and probabilities, and acts accordingly.


And Midjourney?
Another apparent aesthetic counter-argument are the many visual generation tools of which Midjourney is the prime example. The remarkable images these generative models produce seem to have mastered the disconnect. The light behaves. The geometry holds. The shadows fall where shadows ought to fall. One is almost persuaded. One is reminded of Wally discovering, late in the film, that he has become a rather convincing actor. Which is not the same thing as having recovered his sight. What Midjourney has mastered is the aesthetics of plausibility (Su et al., 2025). Through heroic quantities of human feedback, it has learned the statistical grammar of what beautiful images look like. It has learnt the precise pixel distribution that human evaluators label as “a convincing glass of wine” or “a plausible city at night”. It does not know that glass shatters, nor that wine is liquid. It is navigating a latent mapping of human visual taste.

Zhou, Y., Wang, Y., He, X., Xiao, R., Li, Z., Feng, Q., Guo, Z., Yang, Y., Wu, H., Huang, W., Wei, J., Si, D., Yao, X., Bu, J., Huang, H., Fu, T., Tang, S., Fei, B., Zhou, D., … Bai, L. (2025). Scientists’ first exam: Probing cognitive abilities of MLLM via perception, understanding, and reasoning. arXiv Preprint arXiv:2506.10521. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10521
The results are often beautiful, yet in the scientific domain where spatial truth crucial, completely unpredictable. When researchers recently evaluated leading multimodal models on scientific tasks requiring perception, interpretation, and reasoning over real data, performance was strikingly limited. The models achieved only around 30% accuracy, revealing substantial gaps in their ability to integrate visual information with scientific reasoning (Zhou et al., 2025).
The perception may be absent, but the vocabulary remains intact. Wally, as it turns out, knows all the right words for a bar fight.
These failures are not just academic. They are alarming. Engineers developing collaborative tools for blind and low-vision users have discovered that AI-mediated visual description collapses on the very information those users most need: spatial structure (Li et al., 2026). Where is the annotation relative to the diagram? Which cluster corresponds to which label? The visual grammar of arrangement and proximity as semantic signal evaporates in translation. A system that cannot genuinely parse space cannot reconstruct it for the people whose relationship to space is already precarious. Asking Wally to give directions, in other words, has consequences that extend well beyond comedy.

Li, M., Yang, H., Sanda, N., & Das, M. (2026). Idea11y: Enhancing accessibility in collaborative ideation for blind or low vision screen reader users. Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3790878

Wally strides confidently into a bar brawl. Dave is shouting directions — “Left! Duck! Watch out!” Wally borrows Dave’s eyes. Dave borrows Wally’s ears.

When you upload a photo to an AI chatbot, there are essentially two parts working together. A visual system that processes the image — and a language model that does the talking.
And here’s the thing. The language model — the brain part — cannot actually understand images. It’s fundamentally and stubbornly a text system.

So what actually happens? The image gets converted into words first. Into tokens. Then the language model reads those tokens and responds.
So it’s not seeing your photo. It’s reading a description of your photo. And then talking confidently about that description.

The Reality
It is not seeing your photo.
It is reading a description of your photo.
Then talking confidently from that description.
Vision, for most AI systems, is not perception.
It is narration.

That’s the Wally problem. Vision, for most of these AI systems, is not perception. It’s narration.
When things are simple — good lighting, familiar objects — it works well enough. Because the translation from image to words is easy. The system has seen millions of similar examples.
But the moment things get complicated — unusual angles, cluttered scenes, anything that actually requires reasoning about space — the wheels come off.

Simple scenes. Clear lighting. Familiar objects.
The system does well.
Because the translation into words is straightforward.
It has seen millions of similar examples.

When the image is simple — clear lighting, common objects — the system does well. Because it’s seen millions of similar examples. So the translation into words is easy, and the response sounds right.

Novel configurations. Spatial ambiguity. Cluttered scenes.
The visual attention collapses.
The model does what researchers politely call:
“relying on linguistic priors.”

But the moment things get messy — low light, strange angles, unusual situations — that’s when things fall apart.
The visual attention collapses, and the model does what researchers have politely termed “relying on linguistic priors.” Which is a careful way of saying: it stops looking and starts guessing.

The Confabulation
When it isn’t sure, it doesn’t say “I don’t know.”
It guesses.
Confidently.
It knows what usually appears in a kitchen —
so it tells you there’s a microwave on the counter.
Even if there isn’t one.

And here’s the part that should give you pause. When the AI isn’t sure, it doesn’t say “I don’t know.” It guesses. Confidently.
Because it’s trained on patterns of language. It knows what usually appears in a kitchen. So if it sees something vaguely kitchen-like, it might tell you there’s a microwave on the counter. Even if there isn’t one.
It’s not seeing reality. It’s predicting what should be there.

It is not seeing reality.
It is predicting what should be there.
Wally does not merely struggle to see.
He replaces sight with confidence.

Researchers have a polite name for this. They call it relying on linguistic priors. I’d call it: Wally walking confidently into a bar fight he cannot see.
Wally doesn’t merely struggle to see. He actively replaces sight with confidence. And that is exactly what these systems do.

Fair question.

Tesla’s system skips the language step entirely.
Camera → Direct Action (steering, braking, speed)
No words. No narration. Just maths and movement.
In other words:
Dave quietly removed Wally from the vehicle.

Which means, in our film analogy — Dave didn’t fix the problem. He just quietly removed Wally from the vehicle. The blind man isn’t there anymore. So there’s nobody to mislead.

The partnership is all they have.

The Deaf Leading the Blind: What Silicon Valley’s LLMs Cannot See

“…They have mouths, but cannot speak, eyes, but cannot see. They have ears, but cannot hear, noses, but cannot smell… Those who make them will be like them, and so will all who trust in them.” (Psalm 115:4–8, NIV)

I recently found myself watching See No Evil, Hear No Evil — a minor 1989 comedy — on YouTube, drawn in by the “I am white” clip with Richard Pryor (Figure 1). The hilarious Pryor plays Wally, a blind man who flatly refuses to admit it. Gene Wilder plays Dave, a deaf man who has become remarkably good at pretending to hear (Figure 2). Together they blunder through a murder mystery, each borrowing the faculty of the other. Wally strides into bar brawls while Dave shouts directions (Figure 3). Dave borrows Wally’s ears to detect approaching sirens. The comedy turns on the gap between performed and actual perception. On reflection, it could be a surprisingly accurate description of artificial intelligence (AI), specifically visual-focussed Large Language Models (LLMs).







Figure 1: In this subway sequence, Wally (Pryor) performs “simulated sight”, using memorised cues to mask his blindness.








Figure 2: During the job interview, Wally and Dave attempt to communicate across a complete sensory disconnect.








Figure 3: Wally and Dave in a bar brawl.




Silicon Valley has spent the better part of a decade equipping AI with eyes. Visual encoders. Camera inputs. The image-upload button is presented to us with confidence that the machine can now see. What the product announcements rarely discuss is the architecture sitting behind the lens. The LLMs process visual information by first converting it into words, then reasoning about those words, and finally describing what they believe to be there. All with the practised confidence of a man who cannot see the bar fight he has just walked into.


The Wally Problem
Silicon Valley’s flagship general-purpose LLMs still have the language bottleneck firmly in place. The system works, ostensibly, because this partnership is all it has. This is, in essence, a Wally problem. Vision for most multimodal AI systems relies on a process of narration, not perception. Pixels enter; the language model converts them into tokens; the tokens are then reasoned about (Su et al., 2025). Under light cognitive load, this works well enough. Under heavier demands requiring genuine inference, the visual attention collapses, and the model does what researchers have delicately termed “relying on linguistic priors” (Qian et al., 2026). It does a Wally. It narrates the world it expects rather than the one in front of it. In other words, it does not merely struggle to see. It hallucinates with pre-trained confidence.

Qian, Z., Ma, Y., Ouyang, Z., Wang, Z., Xu, Z., Luo, F., Liu, X., Ge, Z., Guo, Y., & Han, J. (2026). Cognitive pivot points and visual anchoring: Unveiling and rectifying hallucinations in multimodal reasoning models. arXiv Preprint arXiv:2604.10219. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10219


But What About Tesla?
An instinctive counter-argument is Tesla. If the LLM cannot see, how then is a two-tonne vehicle able to negotiate Californian roads without incident? The answer is not that Tesla has solved the vision problem. The Tesla v12 architecture maps pixels directly to steering and braking outputs, bypassing language altogether. There is no Dave whispering directions to Wally here. The blind man has simply been removed. The car does not name a stop sign before responding to it; it encodes the sign as a spatial object with associated coordinates and probabilities, and acts accordingly.


And Midjourney?
Another apparent counter-argument is the proliferation of visual generation tools, of which Midjourney is the prime example. The remarkable images these models produce seem to have mastered the disconnect. The light behaves. The geometry holds. The shadows fall where shadows ought to fall. One is almost persuaded. One is reminded of Wally discovering, late in the film, that he has become a rather convincing actor. Which is not the same thing as having recovered his sight. What Midjourney has mastered is the aesthetics of plausibility (Su et al., 2025). Through heroic quantities of human feedback, it has learned the statistical grammar of what beautiful images look like. It has learnt the precise pixel distribution that human evaluators label as “a convincing glass of wine” or “a plausible city at night”. It does not know that glass shatters, nor that wine is liquid. It is navigating a latent mapping of human visual taste.

Zhou, Y., Wang, Y., He, X., Xiao, R., Li, Z., Feng, Q., Guo, Z., Yang, Y., Wu, H., Huang, W., Wei, J., Si, D., Yao, X., Bu, J., Huang, H., Fu, T., Tang, S., Fei, B., Zhou, D., … Bai, L. (2025). Scientists’ first exam: Probing cognitive abilities of MLLM via perception, understanding, and reasoning. arXiv Preprint arXiv:2506.10521. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10521
The results are often beautiful, yet in the scientific domain — where spatial truth is crucial — they are completely unpredictable. When researchers recently evaluated leading multimodal models on scientific tasks requiring perception, interpretation, and reasoning over real data, performance was strikingly limited. The models achieved only around 30% accuracy, revealing substantial gaps in their ability to integrate visual information with scientific reasoning (Zhou et al., 2025).
The perception may be absent, but the vocabulary remains intact. Wally, as it turns out, knows all the right words for a bar fight.
These failures are not just academic. They are alarming. Engineers developing collaborative tools for blind and low-vision users have discovered that AI-mediated visual description collapses on the very information those users most need: spatial structure (Li et al., 2026). Where is the annotation relative to the diagram? Which cluster corresponds to which label? The visual grammar of arrangement — proximity as semantic signal — evaporates in translation. A system that cannot genuinely parse space cannot reconstruct it for the people whose relationship to space is already precarious. Asking Wally to give directions, in other words, has consequences that extend well beyond comedy.

The expansion of multinational dairy processors such as Parmalat, later integrated into the Lactalis Group, has generated allegations of aggressive pricing strategies designed to capture market share from smaller dairies and milk producers, followed by potential recoupment through elevated prices. This synthesis critically evaluates the available evidence across key jurisdictions, particularly South Africa and Australia, within the broader context of agri-food industry consolidation. Drawing on competition authority reports, stakeholder submissions, policy analyses, and peer-reviewed literature in industrial organization and agricultural economics, the review finds that claims of classic predatory pricing—sustained below-cost sales with demonstrable recoupment potential—remain weakly supported and largely unproven under established antitrust standards [1].
In South Africa, Parmalat’s 1998 market entry was associated with a reported price war and downward pressure on raw milk producer prices, with one policy report citing an approximate 28% reduction [2]. However, this evidence is primarily anecdotal and does not include the cost-based or recoupment analyses required to establish predation. In Australia, intense retail discounting (“milk wars”) transmitted price pressure to processors including Parmalat, prompting farmer characterizations of the conduct as predatory; yet the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) determined that such discounting did not constitute predatory pricing and reflected normal competitive dynamics [3], [4].
Available documentation more robustly indicates exercises of buyer (monopsonistic) power over fragmented farmers, occasional horizontal coordination among processors, and structural consolidation driven by retail concentration and scale economies [5], [6]. Methodological limitations—reliance on qualitative testimony, absence of firm-specific variable cost data, and challenges in isolating Parmalat’s conduct from supermarket-led strategies—preclude strong causal attribution to deliberate monopolization via predation. The synthesis concludes that while Parmalat’s operations coincided with accelerated small-producer exits, the evidence better supports broader patterns of buyer power and industry consolidation than legally cognizable predatory pricing. Theoretical implications for antitrust enforcement in agricultural chains and directions for future empirical research are discussed. (242 words)

Introduction
Global dairy processing exhibits pronounced economies of scale, perishability constraints, and dual-sided market power: concentrated retailers upstream and fragmented agricultural producers downstream. Against this backdrop, Parmalat’s international expansion raised concerns regarding potential abuse of dominance through below-cost pricing aimed at eliminating smaller competitors. This synthesis examines whether empirical and documentary sources substantiate allegations of predatory pricing by Parmalat across multiple markets, defined under strategic theory as pricing below an appropriate cost measure (typically average variable cost) with a dangerous probability of recouping losses after rival exit [1].
The analysis adopts an industrial organization lens, distinguishing predatory pricing from related but distinct phenomena: monopsonistic buyer power, horizontal collusion on input prices, and retailer-driven loss-leading. Scope encompasses publicly available materials on South Africa, Australia, and select European contexts, with emphasis on post-liberalization periods. By synthesizing regulatory determinations, stakeholder accounts, and peer-reviewed scholarship, this review highlights evidentiary gaps and situates Parmalat’s conduct within structural transformations of modern agricultural markets [5].

Critical Analysis & Synthesis

Theoretical Framework: Predatory Pricing versus Buyer Power
Predatory pricing doctrine requires demonstration of below-cost pricing, anticompetitive intent or effect (rival exclusion), and recoupment feasibility [1]. In agri-food chains, however, observed price pressures more frequently reflect buyer power, whereby processors or retailers leverage bargaining asymmetry against numerous small suppliers to depress input (farmgate) prices without necessarily engaging in below-cost output sales [5], [6]. Sexton (2013) emphasizes that modern agricultural markets often feature thin trading, asymmetric information, and high search costs, facilitating coordination or unilateral exercises of market power that differ markedly from classic predation models.

[1] P. Bolton, J. F. Brodley, and M. H. Riordan, “Predatory pricing: Strategic theory and legal policy,” Georgetown Law Journal, vol. 88, pp. 2239–2330, 2000.


South African Market Entry and Price Dynamics
Parmalat’s entry into South Africa in 1998 reportedly triggered a price war, with products offered to retailers at reduced rates followed by pressure on producers, resulting in an approximate 28% decline in milk producer prices according to one labor and economic research institute report [2]. This account frames the episode as contributing to sector instability and disproportionate impacts on smaller distributors. Nevertheless, the source constitutes policy advocacy rather than a rigorous empirical study; it lacks detailed cost reconstructions or recoupment analysis. Subsequent investigations by South African authorities more commonly addressed alleged horizontal coordination on raw milk surpluses and pricing among processors, including Parmalat, rather than vertical predation in consumer markets. Such findings align with monopsony concerns over input suppression rather than monopoly power in final goods [5].

[2] Institute for Labour and Economic Research, “Restructuring of the dairy industry: What impact?” ILRIG South Africa, 2020. Available: https://www.ilrigsa.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/restructuring-the-dairy-screen.pdf


Australian Retail-Driven Price Wars and Processor Transmission
In Australia, the 2011 “milk wars” initiated by supermarket private-label discounting generated substantial farmgate price volatility. Farmer submissions to Senate inquiries characterized processor responses—including those involving Parmalat—as patterns likely to eliminate branded products and smaller players, invoking the term “predatory pricing” [4]. The ACCC, however, explicitly found that Coles’ house-brand discounting did not breach competition law or constitute predatory pricing, citing legitimate competitive purposes and insufficient evidence of long-term anticompetitive harm [3]. Processor margins were squeezed as retail bargaining power transmitted lower wholesale prices downstream, illustrating vertical pass-through of buyer power rather than unilateral processor predation. This dynamic underscores the analytical importance of distinguishing supermarket loss-leading from processor strategies [6].

[4] A. P. H. S. E. R. Committee, “Impacts of supermarket price decisions on the dairy industry.” 2011.

[3] Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, “Dairy inquiry,” ACCC, 2017.

[6] Z. Chen, “Buyer power in the theory of industrial organization,” Review of Industrial Organization, 2003, doi: 10.1023/A:1027385122198.


Horizontal Coordination and European Contexts
Evidence of Parmalat/Lactalis involvement appears stronger in horizontal matters, such as alleged coordination on raw milk acquisition in South Africa and information exchange or collusion cases in Spain concerning raw milk supply. These episodes concern buyer-side practices aimed at input price stabilization or suppression, not below-cost consumer sales followed by output price elevation. Such patterns reinforce the monopsony framework articulated in the literature, where processor concentration enables collective influence over fragmented suppliers without satisfying predatory pricing criteria [5].


Structural Drivers of Consolidation
Across jurisdictions, small dairy exits reflect multifaceted pressures: retail concentration, technological advantages (e.g., UHT processing), global commodity volatility, and scale economies favoring large multinationals. Peer-reviewed analyses caution against attributing consolidation predominantly to single-firm predation when systemic factors predominate [5]. The absence of granular, firm-level cost data and longitudinal pricing-recoupment studies across sources limits causal inference regarding Parmalat’s specific role.

[5] R. J. Sexton, “Market power, misconceptions, and modern agricultural markets,” American Journal of Agricultural Economics, vol. 95, no. 2, pp. 209–219, 2013, doi: 10.1093/ajae/aat035.

Discussion
Significant limitations constrain the current evidentiary base. Most materials rely on stakeholder testimony or aggregate trends rather than econometric tests of predation (e.g., difference-in-differences around entry events or margin reconstructions). Distinguishing Parmalat’s conduct from retailer dominance and industry-wide liberalization effects remains challenging. Post-2003 accounting scandal restructuring and Lactalis integration further complicate longitudinal assessment. Future research should prioritize DOI-indexed econometric studies employing administrative cost-price datasets to test recoupment hypotheses more rigorously and compare dairy sub-sectors (fresh pasteurized vs. UHT).
These findings carry policy significance for antitrust in agri-food sectors, where conventional predation standards may undervalue cumulative buyer-power effects. Enhanced supplier protections, such as enforceable dairy codes, warrant consideration alongside preservation of consumer benefits from competitive pricing.

Conclusion
Available sources provide limited corroboration for systematic predatory pricing by Parmalat involving sustained below-cost sales, targeted elimination of small dairies, and subsequent monopoly recoupment. Instead, the record more strongly supports patterns of aggressive competition, monopsonistic pressures on producers, retailer-driven discounting, and structural consolidation in dairy markets. Reframing analysis around buyer power and industry dynamics, rather than classic predation, yields a more defensible and nuanced understanding of Parmalat’s role. Rigorous empirical scholarship remains essential to inform competition policy in global agri-food chains.

[Step back. This is the pivot. It is aimed directly at the people in this room.]

Designers are supposed to be the people in this process who can actually see. Who bring proximity, lived experience, and genuine contextual judgment. That is the job. That is what separates design from decoration.
What is happening instead — in teams and organisations running this at scale every day — is this: designers are loading AI systems with assumptions they already hold. Briefs built from abstraction. Research that confirms what was expected. Insights that have been translated through language before they were ever tested against reality.
Then treating the output as direction.
[pause]

They have simply moved the blindness upstream. And made it invisible.
[pause]
The AI is the clearest mirror the design industry currently has.
What it reflects is not a technology problem.
